Outcome_variable.evidence_source: [/page/8/Text/4] Collectively, self-positive functions of reminiscence (for Identity, Problem-Solving and Death Preparation) may contribute to psychological well-being by restoring, maintaining or enhancing a sense of meaning and purpose in later life (Reker, in press). The stress-buffering and counter-depressive role of meaning in life has been underlined by recent research (Folkman, 1997, 2008), particularly so with older adults (Krause, 2004, 2007). In later life, as lifetime reserves fade, self-positive reminiscences gain importance as bases for the construction of Identity. Reminiscence for Identity typifies this process as this mode of reminiscence entails elaborating a coherent, consistent and meaningful sense of Identity across the adult lifespan. Recalling episodes of Problem-Solving and crisis resolution reaffirm a sense of self-efficacy and control. These memories validate a view of oneself as capable and purposeful. Reminiscences for Death Preparation accompany efforts aimed at deriving a sense of continuity and meaning in one's life, at achieving a serene closure. The influence of self-positive reminiscences on maintaining this positive outlook on self, resulting in lower distress and increased happiness, is achieved, at least in part, via the interplay of assimilative and accommodative coping. On one hand, self-positive reminiscences foster adherence to desired life projections and self-representations (assimilative coping). On the other hand, they participate in the flexible adjustment of goals to actions resources and constraints (accommodative coping). The positive life review that these reminiscences sustain contribute to a multifaceted self-structure embracing a variety of different goals and possible selves. Accommodation is a defensive process that, in later life, becomes a key for maintaining a positive view of self (Brandtsta¨dter, 2006; Frazier et al., 2007). Congruent with this proposition we found that, of the two modes of coping, the accommodative one contributed most to the measurement of coping. Overall, these reminiscences contribute to seeing life goals as meaningful and attractive and enhance the integration of goals into system of meaning. The operation of both coping modes in concert reflects that, in older age, assimilative and accommodative modes of coping complement each other, the; [/page/8/Text/6] In stark contrast, self-negative reminiscences reflect fixed preoccupation with the past: Bitterness Revival denotes preoccupation with unresolved issues, conflicts and lost opportunities; Intimacy Maintenance entails dwelling upon interpersonal losses; and Boredom Reduction expresses longings for better times. Collectively, these self-negative reminiscences typify ruminative coping (i.e. focusing on distressing aspects and meanings in a repetitive and passive manner). This ongoing preoccupation with the past impedes the ability to achieve continuity and meaning as life appears fragmented and purposeless. Repeatedly re-experiencing painful memories impedes adaptation to current life circumstances as finite cognitive and emotional resources are focused on the past, not the present. Psychological distress (anxiety, depression) and unhappiness ensue. This happens because these self-negative reminiscences lead to a breakdown of both assimilative and accommodative coping. Self-negative reminiscences encourage the tenacious adherence to unrealistic goals and performance standards, and to self-destructive projections of life. At the same time, self-negative reminiscences make it difficult to disengage from blocked goals and to relinquish barren life paths and unreachable self-representations. Having difficulties accepting losses, being locked in permanent regrets and perceiving important goals as forever unattainable, all feed helplessness and depression.; [/page/9/Text/11] Regarding the sample, although differences in Depressive Symptomatology and Life Satisfaction between participants who remained in the study and those who abandoned after the first phase were minimal, they suggest that participants who remained in the study at follow-up were a subsample of individuals who reported slightly better mental health functioning.
